title: It Is Sickness Enough to See Death as a Cure
intro: Al-Mutanabbi wrote this in praise of Kafur al-Ikhshidi, who then ran Egypt in the name of Unujur, the son of its former king al-Ikhshid; al-Wahidi dates it to Jumada II 346 AH (957 CE), and its heading in Ibn Jinni's al-Fasr calls it the first poem he greeted Kafur with after leaving Sayf al-Dawla. Al-Barquqi's heading tells the story: the poet left Sayf al-Dawla for Damascus, Kafur wrote inviting him, and when he reached Egypt Kafur gave him a house, robes of honour and thousands of dirhams. The poem opens on a life in which death looks like a cure, urges the self to boldness and pride, and scolds the heart for longing after a faithless friend, whom al-Wahidi takes to be Sayf al-Dawla; this recording stops at line 12, just before the poem turns to Kafur as “a sea at Fustat”. The opening was faulted: al-Tha'alibi, in Yatimat al-Dahr, counts it among the poet's ugly openings and says its talk of sickness, death and fates carries an ill omen that even commoners shy away from, let alone kings. Yet al-Sahib ibn Abbad took nine of its lines, eight of them recited here, into his collection of al-Mutanabbi's proverbial verses.

translation: It is sickness enough to see death as a cure,
and enough for death that it should be wished for.
1.sharh: He speaks to himself: life has reached the point where death looks like the cure, and no illness is worse than one only death heals. When death is longed for, al-Wahidi says, misfortune is complete.

translation: You wished for it when you wished to see
a friend, in vain, or a foe who hides his hate.
2.sharh: He longed for death when he could find neither a true friend nor even an enemy decent enough to hide his hatred. Al-Wahidi says this names the sickness of line 1.

translation: If you are content to live in humiliation,
do not arm yourself with a Yemeni sword.
3.sharh: A sword is carried to ward off humiliation, so a man who accepts humiliation has no use for one. Ibn Jinni notes that the prohibition here does the work of a question.

translation: Do not choose long spears for raiding,
or pick out thoroughbred horses in their prime.
4.sharh: Long spears and fine horses are the gear of a man who will not be wronged; whoever settles for humiliation need not trouble to choose them. Ibn al-Iflili hears in lines 3 and 4 the poet's excuse for leaving Sayf al-Dawla.

translation: Shyness does not save lions from hunger,
and they are not feared until they are fierce.
5.sharh: A lion that keeps modestly to its den goes hungry and unfeared; only the hunter is feared. The parable urges boldness and living by the sword, and al-Ukbari counts it among the finest lines.

translation: I loved you, my heart, before you loved him who went away,
and he was false: so you, be true.
6.sharh: He scolds his heart for pining: he loved it before it loved the man now gone, who proved false, so it must not betray him by longing for that man. Al-Wahidi says he means Sayf al-Dawla.

translation: And I know parting will make you complain when he is gone;
you are not my heart if I see you complain.
7.sharh: He knows his heart will grieve for the friend it was used to, and threatens to disown it if it complains. Al-Ma'arri allows another sense: parting ends the complaint, since despair brings comfort.

translation: For the eye's tears betray their owner
when they run after those who betrayed him.
8.sharh: Weeping for a traitor is loyalty wasted, and loyalty to a traitor betrays oneself, so the tears that run after him betray the man who sheds them. In al-Ukbari's words: keep no faith with the faithless.

translation: When generosity is not spared from harm,
no praise is won and no wealth remains.
9.sharh: A gift spoiled by reproach costs the giver his money and wins him no thanks. Al-Ukbari hears in it the Quran's warning that reproach voids alms; al-Ma'arri hears a jab at the gifts of the man he left.

translation: The soul has traits that show of a man
whether what he gave was generosity or a show of it.
10.sharh: Character gives a man away: it shows whether his giving came from a generous nature or was put on. Ibn Jinni says the poet hints here at a bitter reproach he will not spell out.

translation: Long less, my heart: how often
I have seen you give true love to one untrue.
11.sharh: He tells his heart to stop longing altogether, not merely to long less (al-Barquqi): it has often given its whole love to one whose own love was not true. Al-Ma'arri calls the hint at the man he left all but explicit.

translation: I was made to grow attached: if I journeyed back to youth,
I would leave my grey hair with an aching heart, weeping.
12.sharh: Everyone longs to be rid of grey hair, yet he grows so attached to what he lives with that he would weep to leave even that for youth. Ibn Jinni had heard nothing finer on attachment.

1.1.1-2.meaning: “It suffices you”: the bi- marks the object, not the subject as in the Quran's “God suffices as reckoner”; the subject is “that you see” (Ibn Jinni).

1.2.5.head: أُمنِيَّة
1.2.5.meaning: Wishes: the plural of umniyya, properly amaniyy with a doubled y, here lightened.

2.2.5.head: مُداجٍ
2.2.5.meaning: Mudaji: an enemy who hides his enmity, from duja, darkness.

3.2.4.head: اليَماني
3.2.4.meaning: Yemeni: a sword of Yemeni make; swords were named for Yemen or for India.

4.2.4.head: المُذَكّي
4.2.4.meaning: Madhaki: horses in their prime, whose teeth have all come in.

5.2.5.head: ضارٍ
5.2.5.meaning: Fierce: beasts of prey used to hunting and bold in it.

6.1.1.head: حَبَّ
6.1.1.meaning: I loved you: habbabtu, a rare form of ahbabtu that al-Wahidi calls irregular.

6.1.6.meaning: Went far away: Sayf al-Dawla, the Hamdanid prince of Aleppo, whom the poet had left and does not name (al-Wahidi).

6.2.6.head: وافٍ
6.2.6.meaning: True, faithful. Several commentaries read fa-kun liya wafiya, “be faithful to me”.

7.1.4.head: أَشكى
7.1.4.meaning: Makes you complain. The verb can also mean the opposite, to end a complaint, which gives al-Ma'arri his second reading.

8.1.4.head: غَدور
8.1.4.meaning: Ghudr: treacherous, the plural of ghadur. Some read ghadr, “treachery”.

8.2.4.head: الغادِر
8.2.4.meaning: Those who betrayed. Al-Ukbari's text has al-za'inin, “those who departed”.

8.2.5.head: جارِيَة
8.2.5.meaning: Flowing: jawari, the plural of jariya, here of tears, not its other sense of slave girls.

9.1.6-7.meaning: “From harm”: here, reproaching the receiver with the gift. Al-Ukbari links it with the Quran's “Do not void your alms with reproach and harm” (2:264).

10.2.6.head: تَساخٍ
10.2.6.meaning: Tasakhi: put-on generosity, giving for show.

11.2.6.head: صافٍ
11.2.6.meaning: Pure in love. The editions have jaziya, “one who repays”; two anthologies quote the line with safiya.

12.1.2.head: أَلوف
12.1.2.meaning: Aluf: one who grows attached to whatever he lives with.

12.1.4.head: رَحَلَ
12.1.4.meaning: I journeyed. Some read raja'tu, “I returned”.
